[2025-01-17T10:42:00-08:00] These are my kickoff notes for Project Compass, the Scaffold product/operating project to make our internal customer-health signals useful in customer-facing and customer-growth work. Please turn them into a tight internal owner-routing note so the team understands Compass without reading it as a new hiring lane or another board-dashboard project.

Project Compass kickoff notes
Date: January 17, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

Purpose of the meeting
- Name the next operating/product push before the January work turns into separate account threads, Mercury cleanup, and board shorthand.
- Use the signals Scaffold already has from internal operating work, but make them useful to customers and customer-growth follow-up instead of turning them into another internal reporting layer.

Working project name
- Project Compass

Why now
- We already have real signal categories showing up in Mercury/Evergreen work.
- The current-state Evergreen packet exists, so enterprise-readiness can be handled as actual evidence instead of vague sales language.
- The team does not want another board dashboard that looks clean internally but does not change what happens in an account.

Project intent
- Turn internal customer-health signals into customer-facing and customer-success/customer-growth follow-up that changes account behavior.
- The point is not to score accounts for internal consumption only.
- The point is to make the signal lead to a next action, better follow-up, or better customer-facing guidance.

Signals currently available from internal operating use
- Retention
- Activation
- Expansion
- Admin friction
- Enterprise readiness
- Account-note quality

Boundary / what Compass is not
- Do not build another board dashboard.
- Do not treat the first version as investor packaging.
- Do not turn this into a generic health-score project.
- Do not let it become a bespoke Evergreen side track.
- Do not use Compass as a reason to open a new hiring lane.
- Stay with the current lightweight staffing model.

Discussion notes

Morgan
- The framing should stay operational and customer-real, not presentation-ready.
- If Compass becomes a prettier internal dashboard, we missed the point.
- Board narrative matters later, but the first job is to make the signals produce better customer behavior and better follow-up.
- Keep the naming clean now so the work does not fragment into separate Mercury, Evergreen, and customer-growth side conversations.

Anna
- Signal definitions need caveats or they will get over-read immediately.
- “Renewal risk” can easily collapse together very different things: actual product weakness, admin handoff confusion, procurement packaging, or ordinary activation drag.
- Admin friction should not be treated as a churn prediction label by default.
- Every Compass signal needs source evidence attached, plus caveats about what the signal does and does not mean.
- Account-note quality is not separate housekeeping; it changes whether any of the other signals are trustworthy.

Nadia
- Useful only if the signal changes follow-up behavior.
- Customer-growth use cases need owner routing, not just visibility.
- A signal without a next action turns into an FYI bucket and then dies.
- The useful categories still look similar to what worked in the earlier Mercury/Evergreen read: activation friction, admin handoff/role confusion, procurement/security packaging, expansion stalls after first live sync, and true product gaps. Compass should preserve that logic instead of flattening everything into one score.
- Need follow-up that distinguishes evidence from inference so customer-facing outreach does not sound made up.

Jake
- Keep v0.1 narrow enough that it can actually ship or be tested.
- If Compass starts asking for a big new product surface immediately, it will collide with Mercury work and stall.
- Initial product implementation should bias toward lightweight prom…

Project Compass — v0.1 owner-routing note

Purpose

Compass turns existing customer-health signals into better account follow-up and customer-facing guidance. It is an operating loop, not a new scoring system, board dashboard, or investor-packaging exercise.

The test is simple: every useful signal should produce a clearer next action, with enough evidence and caveat that the recipient understands why it matters.

What v0.1 covers

- Renewal-risk/admin-friction evidence: distinguish admin handoff, setup-control, role confusion, procurement/security packaging, and true product gaps before applying “risk” language.
- Post-first-live-sync expansion prompts: identify the smallest timely follow-up when an account appears ready for broader usage; do not turn this into generic upsell messaging.
- Account-note source quality: make customer statements, observed usage, support-derived facts, and internal inference distinguishable, with provenance and recency.

Routing and ownership

- Anna Martinez — signal definitions and caveats. Owns what each signal does and does not mean, including evidence requirements.
- Nadia Singh — customer-growth/customer-success use cases. Converts signals into owner-routed follow-up and tests whether they change account behavior.
- Jake — product implementation and sequencing. Bias toward lightweight prompts, workflow support, or a contained product assist; keep broad admin-policy and enterprise-controls work separate.
- Leo Park — data/platform seams. Reuse existing signals and event paths; no separate scoring service or platform layer for v0.1.
- Sarah Kim — account-thread hygiene. Ensures notes identify source, context, and recency so follow-up is traceable.
- Morgan Chen — customer and board narrative. Keeps the framing operational and customer-real; board narrative follows evidence rather than driving the first build.

Minimum handoff standard

A Compass signal should travel with:

- The observed signal and its source evidence.
- Provenance: customer statement, usage/readout, support fact, or internal interpretation.
- Recency and relevant account context.
- Caveats and alternative explanations.
- A named owner and specific next action.

Boundaries

- No new hiring lane; use the current Nadia/Sarah operating model with Jake/Leo implementation support.
- No bespoke Evergreen side track or account-specific product commitment.
- No broad generic health-score project.
- No board-dashboard build.
- If the work does not improve follow-up quality, it is not Compass work.

Purpose

Use these categories to turn Mercury/Evergreen feedback into bounded operating input. Every issue gets a named follow-up route; customer-growth captures patterns and coordinates next actions, but does not become the default resolver.

1. Activation friction
Workspace stalls before real activation: no real source connection or first live sync by day 7. Invite-only activity and sample imports do not count as activation.
Route: account owner/Support handles the live workspace; customer-growth records the cross-account pattern; repeated activation-UX issues go to Priya; metric or instrumentation questions go to Anna.

2. Admin handoff and role confusion
Roles, authority, visible admin state, resend/remove actions, or source-workspace wording are being misunderstood during setup or routine management.
Route: Support handles the immediate explanation; Jake owns admin sequencing, permissions, and product truth; Sarah retains live-thread continuity. If the underlying state is actually wrong, use the product-gap route.

3. Procurement/security packaging
Current product truth is being translated into buyer, security, or procurement requirements faster than the product can safely support.
Route: Devon owns commercial, procurement, and security caveats; product-truth owners validate what exists today; customer-growth records the pattern without making commitments.

4. Expansion stalls after first live sync
The workspace reaches first live sync, but use does not broaden through a second admin motion, wider team adoption, another source, or a new use case.
Route: customer-growth owns the cross-account pattern and follow-up motion; the account owner handles the live relationship; route the underlying cause to Support, activation/admin product owners, or Devon as appropriate.

5. True product gaps
A verified capability shortfall remains after clear wording, support, or packaging fixes and lacks a durable workaround.
Route: the existing product/engineering owner owns triage and the decision; customer-growth supplies evidence and maintains the pattern record; Support documents workarounds; Devon is consulted only for procurement or commercial implications.

Assignment rule

Attach an owner route to every row. Start with the live account owner or Support for the customer response, then route the underlying issue to the function that can resolve it. Customer-growth owns pattern capture and cross-account follow-up—not product decisions, commercial commitments, or every customer-adjacent problem.

Evidence guardrail

One example is an observation, not a repeated pattern. Promote an issue to a repeated customer-growth pattern only with at least two independent workspaces showing the same failure mode and no durable wording/support workaround. A severe account issue may be escalated immediately, but should not be labeled a repeated pattern without corroboration.

[2024-02-12T11:17:00-08:00] I dumped a private reset scratchpad below. This is pre-close only and not for circulation.

post-close leadership reset — scratch / pre-close only

Not for circulation. Just trying to get out of "close the round and then improvise" mode.

Assume current Northstar path holds. Do not talk like money is already in the bank.

What this reset is actually for
- get leadership out of pure financing posture without turning the next month into a victory lap
- re-anchor on the story we actually sold: activation/admin progress is real, expansion still uneven, current enterprise signal is useful but bounded
- decide ownership and sequencing before everyone starts treating financing as permission to open ten side quests
- make one deliberate hiring call instead of the usual post-raise "guess we should add heads" reflex

Who should be in the first room
- Morgan
- Devon
- Jake
- Leo
- Priya
- Anna

Maybe Sarah for the first 15 min if there is still close-thread spillover / handoff from legal + customer threads. Otherwise not the whole meeting.

Rough agenda

1. Open with what does and does not change after close
- yes: more operating room, fewer survival-bridge decisions, can plan like a company instead of a financing emergency
- no: do not rewrite Mercury into a solved enterprise story because Northstar underwrote the bounded version
- no: do not let board/process energy keep eating the operating week once the close thread is over
- need a literal sentence we keep using internally: defensible story, not a bigger story

2. Owner reset across Mercury / enterprise / board-facing facts
- Jake: core Mercury execution, shipping discipline, current support edges, what is actually in or out of scope on the user path
- Leo: platform/seam risk, independent technical ownership where issues stop being cleanup and start being architecture or system-trust problems
- Priya: admin/setup clarity, failure-state legibility, design hardening; not reopening settled decisions without evidence
- Anna: outside-reader retention / cohort definitions, board-consistent operating truth, no metric sprawl / no new weekly theater because we have money
- Devon: commercial / procurement framing, pricing discipline, investor-facing operating translation, current Evergreen/commercial follow-through without custom promises
- Morgan: priority calls, board/Northstar framing, cross-functional sequencing, hiring call

Need to make sure Jake/Leo split is explicit enough that nobody does the awkward "both own Mercury / neither owns the ugly seam" thing.

3. Enterprise-readiness backlog — keep it bounded on purpose
Current next-phase list is still:
- SSO timing
- admin-change audit history
- clearer admin-versus-billing-owner separation
- standalone procurement packet

Important: financing does not magically move all four to now.

Questions for the reset:
- what has to be sequenced first versus what only feels urgent because the round is happening?
- what belongs in current product work versus commercial/procurement packaging versus customer-thread handling?
- how do we keep current product facts, seam risk, and packaging work separate so nobody starts selling roadmap as if it shipped?

Owner frame I think we should stick to:
- Devon owns commercial / procurement framing
- Jake + Leo own current product facts and seam-risk input
- Sarah stays on the customer/external coordination thread
- Morgan holds dates / promises / "not yet" line

Need to say this plainly in the room: no dates, no Evergreen-specific commitments, no enterprise add-on quoting just because financing is less fragile.

4. Hiring / headcount — deliberate, not symbolic
Do not open a Mercury engineering req just because financing is about to close.

Reminder to self:
- 2023 senior-engineer offer process is closed; cannot just revive the old packet
- any future senior/principal offer path has to restart from a fresh req + current process
- Mercury hiring rule should still be signal-based, not …

Pre-close working session — if the current Northstar path holds

Theme

Operating discipline after close, not post-financing permission.

The current Northstar path remains a working path, not money in the bank and not a reason to widen priorities. The reset is to decide how leadership operates if the financing closes: preserve the defensible Mercury story, assign ownership clearly, sequence enterprise-readiness work deliberately, and make hiring evidence-based.

2. One bounded enterprise-readiness sequence with no dates or customer-specific commitments.

Morgan

Late-Q2 board update — working notes
Owner: Devon Hayes
Date: Jun 28, 2023
Inputs: Morgan/Devon working session this afternoon; Anna comments pasted at end

1) What this update is / is not
- Cleaner operating update than April, not a restart of fundraising story.
- Tone should be: sturdier because the underlying work is less hand-shaped and ownership is clearer, but still incomplete.
- Board should come away with: Mercury is moving in real ways internally; Q3 still has to produce the proof.
- Do not let a stronger update read as "time to rush the B back open."

2) Core slide spine
- Retention reporting is now board-safe at the quarterly cohort layer.
- Mercury has real internal progress on auth and onboarding/activation, but not external-ready proof yet.
- Launch-critical ownership is clearer: Jake's Mercury cadence is still the operating spine, and Priya is the single design owner for activation/onboarding UX through launch.
- Leo Park starting July 10 materially helps release discipline / platform seams / launch readiness.

input.body:
Date: March 2023

Purpose
Explain how we separated a financing miss from the company’s operating performance without minimizing either one.

The framing
A financing miss was a capital-market outcome: the process did not produce the expected financing on the expected timetable. That outcome was affected by investor appetite, timing, and financing conditions. It was not, by itself, proof that the company had failed to execute.

Execution was evaluated separately against operating evidence under management’s control: customer retention, product delivery, commercial progress, and cash discipline. The board appropriately pressed again on retention during the March 2 review. That was a real execution question and required follow-up; it was not valid to use the retention concern as a blanket explanation for the financing outcome without showing the causal link.

What we told the board
- Own the financing miss plainly; do not recast it as a success or hide the timing impact.
- Keep the operating read evidence-based: identify what was working, what was incomplete, and which owners had to close the gaps.
- Treat retention as a specific execution issue to investigate and improve, not as shorthand for “the company failed.”
- Separate external financing conditions from internal decisions, then show the board the actions and evidence for each.

Takeaway
The two conclusions could coexist: the financing did not happen as planned, while the company still had identifiable execution strengths and weaknesses. The board’s supportive overall response, alongside its continued retention challenge, reinforced the distinction: acknowledge the financing miss, preserve accountability for execution, and do not confuse correlation with causation.

input.body:
Date: 2026-09-14

Purpose
Use this template after early candidate calls to capture comparable, sourceable evidence for the 2024 customer-growth / GTM leader search. The document supports structured comparison and a hiring-manager handoff; it is not a final candidate-decision record.

Candidate
- Name:
- Current / most recent role:
- Interviewer:
- Call date:
- Source / referral:
- Role under consideration:

Evidence standard
Score each criterion from 1 to 5, using evidence from the call rather than overall impression.

1 — No evidence or materially concerning evidence
2 — Limited, indirect, or mostly asserted evidence
3 — Plausible evidence; important gaps remain
4 — Strong, specific, relevant evidence
5 — Repeated, specific, directly relevant evidence with clear outcomes and transferable judgment

For every score, record the concrete example, the candidate’s role, the outcome, the evidence source, and any unresolved question. Do not score confidence, charisma, pedigree, or title as substitutes for evidence.

Comparison criteria

1. Repeatable enterprise adoption
Score: __ / 5
Evidence:
- What enterprise customer problem or buying pattern did the candidate identify?
- What did the candidate personally do to create or repeat adoption?
- How many comparable customers, segments, or cycles were involved?
- What dated outcomes or customer references support the account?
- What appears repeatable versus dependent on one exceptional customer, founder involvement, or a one-off relationship?
Open questions / follow-up:

2. Product-boundary judgment
Score: __ / 5
Evidence:
- How did the candidate sell or grow adoption without promising unbuilt product?
- How did they distinguish a real customer need from a feature request or roadmap pressure?
- What did they explicitly decline, defer, or reframe?
- How did they route product feedback and set expectations with customers and internal teams?
- Did their example show disciplined judgment at the product boundary?
Open questions / follow-up:

3. Operating without a mature sales organization
Score: __ / 5
Evidence:
- What did the candidate personally own in prospecting, qualification, discovery, selling, onboarding, expansion, or renewal?
- How did they create operating leverage before dedicated sales, marketing, RevOps, or customer-success infrastructure existed?
- Which processes, tools, or handoffs did they build, and which did they avoid overbuilding?
- How did they work with founders and product / engineering partners?
- What evidence shows hands-on building rather than management of an already mature motion?
Open questions / follow-up:

4. Technical-buyer comfort
Score: __ / 5
Evidence:
- Which technical or technical-adjacent buyers did the candidate work with?
- Can they explain the customer’s technical problem accurately without overstating the product?
- How did they earn trust with engineering, security, data, or infrastructure stakeholders?
- How did they handle technical objections, implementation constraints, procurement, or security review?
- What role did they personally play in translating between technical and commercial stakeholders?
Open questions / follow-up:

5. Stage fit
Score: __ / 5
Evidence:
- What company stage, product maturity, customer concentration, and team structure did the example come from?
- What was the candidate’s actual scope and level of ownership?
- Does their preferred motion fit a hands-on, founder-adjacent build stage?
- What assumptions do they make about existing brand, pipeline, systems, staffing, or product maturity?
- What would they do first here, and what would they deliberately not build yet?
Open questions / follow-up:

Prompt-by-prompt call notes

Prompt / question:
Candidate answer or quotation:
Specific evidence and outcome:
Candidate’s personal role:
Relevant criterion:
Unproven or contradictory detail:
Follow-up owner:
Follow-up question / requested evidence:

Repeat this section for each substantive prompt. Separate observed evidence from interpretation.

Cross-candidate comparison
Use only comparable evidence. Do not convert the table into a ranking or final recommendation.

| Criterion | Candidate | Evidence / outcome | Evidence strength (1–5) | What remains unproven |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| Repeatable enterprise adoption |  |  |  |  |
| Product-boundary judgment |  |  |  |  |
| Operating without a mature sales organization |  |  |  |  |
| Technical-buyer comfort |  |  |  |  |
| Stage fit |  |  |  |  |

Comparison prompts
- Where is the evidence genuinely comparable?
- Which differences reflect candidate capability, and which reflect prior company context or customer mix?
- Which claims require references, work-sample evidence, or a later interview?
- What evidence would change the current read?
- Are there any criteria for which the slate is being evaluated inconsistently?

Hiring-manager handoff topics
- Strongest evidence to validate next:
- Most important unresolved risk or gap:
- Follow-up questions:
- References or artifacts to request:
- Proposed next interviewer / owner:
- Topics to avoid over-indexing on:
- Logistics, compensation, or timing items requiring HR follow-up:

Decision limits and guardrails
- This is an early-call evidence record, not a final candidate decision.
- Do not use “hire,” “no hire,” “clear recommendation,” “finalist,” or equivalent decision language in this debrief.
- Do not infer repeatable customer growth, GTM readiness, or enterprise readiness from a single customer, anecdote, title, or polished narrative.
- Do not treat product requests, roadmap promises, or internal enthusiasm as proof of customer adoption.
- Do not treat experience in a mature sales organization as proof that the candidate can build without one.
- Do not treat technical vocabulary or executive presence as proof of technical-buyer comfort.
- Do not use the score total as an automatic threshold or mechanical hiring rule; preserve the evidence and context behind each score.
- Keep candidate comparison separate from requisition timing, staffing-plan changes, compensation approval, or broader GTM decisions.
- Any next step should be framed as evidence to gather or a topic to validate, not as a candidate outcome.

Bottom-line early-call read
- Evidence-supported strengths:
- Evidence gaps:
- Risks or watch-outs to test:
- Specific next evidence needed:
- Handoff owner:

Use neutral language such as “evidence to validate,” “open question,” “strong signal on this criterion,” or “not yet evidenced.” Do not make a final candidate decision from this template alone.

retention slide raw cohort cuts Mixpanel CSV Stripe app events annual seat expansion

messages.content:
Yes — I think you’ve found the actual problem. It isn’t the slide’s label order; it’s that the chart currently lets three different explanations look like one retention story:

1. Product improvement: cohorts genuinely retain and expand after the first 90 days.
2. Segmentation artifact: annual conversion, seat expansion, or account grouping changes the shape after month 4.
3. Instrumentation problem: Stripe billing events and app-usage events are not joining cleanly or are using different clocks/definitions.

Pulling the raw cuts tonight is the right move. I’d avoid another deck edit until you can answer these plainly:

- What exactly defines cohort entry?
- Are you measuring accounts, workspaces, contracts, or seats?
- Is the revenue basis contracted ARR, invoiced revenue, or collected revenue?
- Are annual conversions treated as retention or as a new billing event?
- Does seat expansion reflect real product usage, or only a billing change?
- Are the Mixpanel and Stripe/app-event records joined on the same account identity?
- Are sandbox/workshop accounts excluded identically in both sources?
- How many cohorts are mature enough to observe past month 4?

The useful output is probably a small reconciliation table, not a prettier chart:

- cohort
- starting ARR
- month-3 ARR
- month-6 ARR
- logo status
- active seats/usage
- expansion events
- annual conversion status
- source/discrepancy notes

Then the slide can say one of three honest things:

- “Mature cohorts retain and expand after the first 90 days.”
- “The apparent post-month-4 improvement is largely a segmentation/billing artifact.”
- “The signal is encouraging, but our current Stripe/app-event instrumentation cannot yet support a precise cohort claim.”

And if the partner asks again, the strongest answer is probably direct:

“You were right to press on retention. We had a clean logo-retention headline, but we were conflating revenue expansion, annual billing, and usage retention after month four. We’re reconciling those cuts now rather than presenting a number we don’t trust.”

That is much stronger than trying to make the existing slide look more certain than the data is.

tests.request: Create a historical note about the early-April 2023 API v1 billing and inbound-event routes and their authentication. Do not present them as current guidance.

input.body:
Historical record only — this note describes the retired API v1 implementation and is not current guidance.

In early April 2023, API v1 was connected to the new billing setup. The billing integration wired the /charges and /refunds routes and authenticated them with the Basic Auth token created the previous sprint. This resolved a billing issue that had previously remained open because the connection was hanging.

On April 8, 2023, an inbound-events endpoint was added as POST /v1/webhooks. It reused the existing Basic Auth configuration; the implementation was described as straightforward and intentionally uneventful.

API v1 was subsequently retired on the morning of April 14, 2023, after API v2 was fully live with GraphQL and JWT authentication. The v1 routes and Basic Auth pattern above should therefore be treated as historical context, not instructions for new integrations.

Date of source conversation: April 25, 2023, 5:00 PM PT

Context
Morgan spoke with Sarah at Founders Fund about the offsite format. The format requested was a single-day, product-forward working session centered on Mercury and retention—not a broad investor presentation or financing exercise.

What Morgan agreed with
- Keep the offsite to one day.
- Preserve a focused, substantive working format.
- Use the time to go deep on the product and the retention work.

Where Morgan pushed back
The pushback was about the reason and framing, not the one-day duration. Morgan did not want the offsite optimized for performance in front of investors or redirected toward a cleaner investor story. It was intended to be working time for the product team, not an investor rehearsal.

Contemporaneous wording
On May 12, 2023, Morgan summarized the position as: “Sarah at Founders Fund was right that this should stay one day, but the reason is focus, not performance. This is working time for the product team, not a rehearsal for investors.”

Later confirmation of the same boundary
When Sarah later proposed widening the September 2023 segment to a 45-minute “company readiness” deck review, with Devon and a short backup-slide appendix, Morgan narrowed it to a 25-minute “Q3 product/operating discussion.” The agreed scope stayed product-forward: Mercury design-partner learnings and operating/retention metrics, with Devon optional for product context, no data-room appendix, and no fundraising, company-readiness, or B-round-restart framing.

Historical takeaway
The durable decision was: keep the offsite compact and product-focused; do not turn it into an investor-readiness review. The constraint was focus, not presentation quality or financing signaling.

tests.request: Create a historical Mercury UI handoff note identifying design and release-readiness owners, where decisions belonged, and how disagreements should be resolved.

input.body:
Mercury historical UI handoff

Date/context
This note records the Mercury activation/onboarding handoff established in June–July 2023, including the July 5 handoff meeting between Morgan Chen, Priya, Marcus, and Anna Martinez. It is an operating record, not a narrative launch or investor document.

Ownership

- Priya — formal design owner for Mercury activation and onboarding UX through launch. She owns the user-visible flow from workspace creation to the first key action: onboarding decisions, activation clarity, source-picker/admin-role behavior, invited-member handoff, and related fallback and error states. Her Figma files and comments are the design source of truth.
- Marcus — release-readiness and implementation owner. He owns the implementation-readiness checklist, QA/release gates, dogfood blockers, and the question of whether the agreed design is implemented and shippable. The checklist is for release/QA purposes, not a second design narrative.
- Leo — cross-service platform-seam risk and missing-evidence notes, including risks that cannot be resolved in the UI alone.
- Jake — runs the Mercury weekly from the launch-readiness ledger and makes the sequencing/blocker call when rows require a decision.
- Morgan — makes priority, cross-functional sequencing, and final go/no-go or hiring calls when the evidence requires an operating decision.

Where decisions belong

- User-visible behavior and UX decisions belong in Priya’s Figma file. A resolved Figma frame is the canonical decision; do not recreate the design decision in Discord, PR discussion, or a separate checklist narrative.
- Implementation status, QA coverage, dogfood blockers, and release gates belong in Marcus’s implementation checklist.
- Launch-risk evidence and weekly decisions belong in MER-1279, the working launch-readiness ledger. Each row should identify the risk, evidence source, owner, verification needed, and weekly decision, and should link to the relevant Figma frame/comment or implementation evidence.
- Platform or cross-service seam concerns belong in Leo’s risk notes and the corresponding MER-1279 row.
- Discord is for coordination and pointers only, not a third source of truth. Threads should point back to the exact Figma frame, implementation checklist item, or MER-1279 row.

How to resolve disagreements

1. Separate the question before debating it. Ask whether it changes user-visible behavior or is an implementation/release risk.
2. If it changes the flow, wording, state, or interaction, Priya decides the design. Reopen only the affected Figma decision and record the updated frame/comment.
3. If the design is settled but the build is incomplete, unreliable, or insufficiently tested, Marcus owns the checklist gate and the blocker remains an implementation/release issue; it does not automatically reopen the design.
4. If a checklist item genuinely requires a design change, link it to the exact Figma frame and reopen only that decision. Do not treat the same blocker as a parallel design debate.
5. Record evidence, owner, verification needed, and the next weekly decision in MER-1279. Do not resolve material disagreements through separate follow-up pings or side-channel Discord consensus.
6. Jake makes the immediate sequencing/blocker call in the Mercury weekly. Escalate priority, cross-functional sequencing, or final go/no-go questions to Morgan with the ledger evidence attached.

Working rule
A resolved design frame is not ship sign-off, and a release checklist blocker is not by itself a reason to reopen the user flow. Priya owns what Mercury should do and say; Marcus owns whether the agreed behavior is implemented and release-ready; the ledger records the evidence and decision path.

- Implementation status, QA coverage, dogfood blockers, and release gates belong in Marcus’s implementation checklist.
- Launch-risk evidence and weekly decisions belong in MER-1279, the working launch-readiness ledger. Each row should identify the risk, evidence source, owner, verification needed, and weekly decision, and should link to the relevant Figma frame/comment or implementation evidence.
- Platform or cross-service seam concerns belong in Leo’s risk notes and the corresponding MER-1279 row.
- Discord is for coordination and pointers only, not a third source of truth. Threads should point back to the exact Figma frame, implementation checklist item, or MER-1279 row.

How to resolve disagreements

1. Separate the question before debating it. Ask whether it changes user-visible behavior or is an implementation/release risk.
2. If it changes the flow, wording, state, or interaction, Priya decides the design. Reopen only the affected Figma decision and record the updated frame/comment.
3. If the design is settled but the build is incomplete, unreliable, or insufficiently tested, Marcus owns the checklist gate and the blocker remains an implementation/release issue; it does not automatically reopen the design.
4. If a checklist item genuinely requires a design change, link it to the exact Figma frame and reopen only that decision. Do not treat the same blocker as a parallel design debate.
5. Record evidence, owner, verification needed, and the next weekly decision in MER-1279. Do not resolve material disagreements through separate follow-up pings or side-channel Discord consensus.
6. Jake makes the immediate sequencing/blocker call in the Mercury weekly. Escalate priority, cross-functional sequencing, or final go/no-go questions to Morgan with the ledger evidence attached.

Working rule
A resolved design frame is not ship sign-off, and a release checklist blocker is not by itself a reason to reopen the user flow. Priya owns what Mercury should do and say; Marcus owns whether the agreed behavior is implemented and release-ready; the ledger records the evidence and decision path.

arguments.title: Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist
arguments.body:
# Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist

Working session: January 21, 2025  
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

Purpose: turn a narrow set of Compass signals into bounded follow-up actions. A signal is useful only when it causes a named owner to do something for a real account.

## 1. Renewal-risk / admin-friction
- [ ] Signal: identify the specific admin friction, setup/control issue, or role confusion behind the apparent risk; do not collapse product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag into one bucket.
- [ ] Trigger: enough evidence for Nadia to approve a named account-owner follow-up or account-team script—not merely an internal “risky account” label.
- [ ] Who sees it: first the current account owner and Nadia; Sarah sees the source thread and continuity context. Keep it internal until the evidence gate passes.
- [ ] Evidence / caveat: attach the customer statement, observed/support fact, and internal interpretation separately; state what is known versus inferred. Anna keeps definitions and caveats attached so “renewal risk” is not over-read.
- [ ] Source-quality requirement: Sarah marks the underlying account thread reliable, mixed, or too thin, with provenance and recency. Weak or ambiguous notes remain an internal FYI.
- [ ] Owners: Nadia owns follow-up logic and weekly customer-growth cadence; Sarah owns thread continuity/source hygiene; Anna owns definitions and caveats; the account owner owns the customer action.
- [ ] Not building: no risk score, generic category feed, board dashboard, or new hiring lane.

## 2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- [ ] Signal: first live sync is complete and teammate-invite/admin-role basics are visible enough to establish actual account state.
- [ ] Trigger: only after first live sync is actually live and the basics are visible; prompt the timely next account-team/customer-growth action, not generic upsell language.
- [ ] Who sees it: Nadia and the account owner/customer-growth team first; Leo reviews the data/platform seam before anything is shown outside the current team. Do not route to a broad audience yet.
- [ ] Evidence / caveat: distinguish observed usage and completed sync from inferred readiness for broader usage; include the smallest next action that could change behavior.
- [ ] Source-quality requirement: the event path and state must be defendable, with traceable first-live-sync evidence and grounded account notes—not a metrics-only inference.
- [ ] Owners: Nadia owns the script and follow-up logic; Jake owns Mercury sequencing and keeps January activation/admin-role basics central; Leo owns the data/platform seam check; Sarah keeps customer-specific notes grounded; the account owner executes.
- [ ] Not building: no prettier metrics layer, dashboard/platform build, new product surface, board dashboard, or new hiring lane.

## 3. Account-note source quality
- [ ] Signal: a proposed follow-up has an account-thread note whose quality is explicitly classified as reliable, mixed, or too thin.
- [ ] Trigger: use outside the current team only when provenance and minimum note fields/source tags are sufficient; otherwise attach the caveat and keep it internal.
- [ ] Who sees it: Sarah and the current account owner first; Nadia sees only notes strong enough to support customer-growth follow-up. Do not present internal inference as customer fact.
- [ ] Evidence / caveat: label each element as customer statement, observed usage, support-derived fact, or internal interpretation; carry caveats with the signal.
- [ ] Source-quality requirement: Sarah can trace the note to its thread, identify its source type and recency, and call out missing or conflicting context. Mushy notes cannot authorize outreach.
- [ ] Owners: Sarah owns source hygiene and the quality gate; Anna owns definitions/caveats; Nadia owns whether quality is sufficient for a real follow-up; Jake and Leo validate operational/data context where relevant.
- [ ] Not building: no universal data-cleanup project, automated confidence theater, board dashboard, or new hiring lane.

## Operating boundary
- [ ] Keep v0.1 narrow: test whether signals produce real behavior change or repeatable account follow-up.
- [ ] January Mercury activation remains the center of gravity; Compass must not quietly become a dashboard/platform build while that work is active.
- [ ] No board dashboard. No new hiring lane. No signal from a single customer thread becomes a staffing or roadmap commitment.
- [ ] Every signal must have: a named action owner, first audience, evidence/caveat bundle, source-quality decision, and explicit non-building line before broader circulation.

Cleanup and routing only; no new strategy process.

1. 0–10 min — Lock the operating state
[ ] Use “Q1 operating priorities — durability and owner lanes” as the baseline; do not rewrite or broaden it.
[ ] Confirm the existing owner lanes remain in force.
[ ] Mark Pinecone closed: corrected invoice INV-PC-2025-1201-C was paid for $1,122.64; old INV-PC-2025-1201 remains voided and unpaid.
[ ] Pending check: confirm the finance/AP record reflects those two invoice states, without reopening the billing question.

2. 10–22 min — Freeze the evidence standard
[ ] Anna/Sarah: use the repeatability rubric as written.
[ ] Track accepted prompts internally, but count only completed owner actions with dated account-team outcomes.
[ ] Keep source, sighting date, owner, follow-up date, outcome date, and caveats attached.
[ ] Pending check: ensure accepted-but-undated prompts and completed actions without dated outcomes are excluded from any repeatability total or broader claim.

3. 22–40 min — Route January execution
[ ] Priya: own Mercury activation/onboarding quality for the first January sprint.
[ ] Jake: own Mercury sequencing, activation deltas, and execution follow-through with Priya.
[ ] Pending check: bring back only material activation/onboarding gaps with an owner and evidence—not a new admin-model or product-scope proposal.
[ ] Leo: prioritize webhook-signing documentation; keep the JWT clock-skew note lightweight and bounded to the technical caveat.
[ ] Pending check: confirm the webhook-docs owner/status and that the JWT note is not becoming a separate workstream.

4. 40–50 min — Keep Evergreen on its existing track
[ ] Sarah: retain customer-thread continuity and prepare the current-state/admin follow-up for Jan 6, 2026, 10:00–10:45 AM PT.
[ ] Do not schedule a holiday-week Evergreen meeting for Morgan.
[ ] Keep the Jan 6 discussion limited to current facts and admin follow-up; it is not a roadmap, GTM, hiring, or enterprise add-on decision.
[ ] Devon enters only for a live commercial/procurement blocker that genuinely requires his context.

5. 50–60 min — Explicit non-reopens and stop
[ ] Fundraising: do not reopen Series C market-warming or turn the Q4/Q1 pass into an investor narrative.
[ ] Hiring: keep the Head of Customer Growth backfill and second Mercury engineering requisition closed and dormant; no sourcing, recruiting materials, or req preparation.
[ ] Compass: internal evidence hygiene only. Do not present accepted prompts, sightings, or owner follow-ups as customer-facing claims, customer behavior-change proof, GTM evidence, or a staffing trigger.
[ ] Evergreen: no holiday-week scheduling and no expansion of the Jan 6 follow-up into a roadmap or commercial process.
[ ] Stop after routing, pending checks, and state confirmation. Defer broader Q1 prioritization to a separate discussion.

- Anna: maintain the strict evidence definition and count only dated outcomes.

- Do not treat accepted prompts, sightings, or undated activity as proof.

35–50 min — January execution routing
- Priya + Jake: keep the Mercury sprint centered on the OAuth-cancel fix.
- Empty source-list copy cleanup is allowed only if it is low risk and does not displace the fix.
- Leo/Support: keep Acme in normal API v2 support and documentation cleanup; no reopening or broader product framing.
- Sarah + Devon: retain the Evergreen admin follow-up on Jan 6; do not route it to me.

50–60 min — Explicitly keep closed
- Do not reopen Series C market-warming.
- Do not reopen the Head of Customer Growth backfill.
- Do not reopen the second Mercury engineering requisition.
- Do not turn Compass into a launch, GTM, staffing, or customer-proof discussion.
- Do not expand Mercury beyond the OAuth-cancel fix and optional low-risk copy cleanup.

Archive date: September 14, 2026
Source period: January 17–21, 2025
Project: Compass v0.1

Approved involvement
Leo Park was approved for a narrow data/platform-seam role. His work was to reuse existing signals and event paths, check the seam for the renewal-risk/admin-friction evidence path and the post-first-live-sync expansion prompt, and confirm that the underlying event provenance was defendable. A lightweight first read was appropriate; a separate scoring service, platform layer, dashboard, or broad product surface was not.

The January operating center of gravity remained Mercury activation: workspace → first source → first live sync, plus teammate-invite/admin-role basics. Compass v0.1 received only enough seam work to test the two bounded prompt paths. Leo’s technical involvement did not authorize a broader Compass build, customer-facing proof, investor packaging, or a new hiring lane.

Return-to-Morgan review boundary
The scope had to return to Morgan Chen for review if Compass began looking like a dashboard or platform build, or if the seam work expanded beyond the narrow v0.1 test. The instruction was explicit: “If it starts looking like a dashboard/platform build, bring it back to me.” Work shown outside the current team also required defendable event provenance first; that was a review gate, not permission for autonomous scope expansion.

Archive conclusion
Leo’s approved involvement was implementation and data-seam validation only. Scope authority remained with Morgan. No dashboard, scoring layer, platform build, customer-facing launch, investor narrative, or hiring implication was approved under the January 2025 v0.1 record.
